1. The animation shows how inflation wears down what a fixed income can buy. Three illustrative retirees each get the same 2% raise. Edna starts in Jan 1949, Ruth in Aug 2006, and Carl in Jan 1966. Each has a row of crates, which stand for what their income buys. The frames use US consumer price (CPI-U) history and are labeled "history, not a forecast."

2. In frames 1–2, all three rows start out full, and Carl's and Ruth's rows begin to dim at the right end. By frame 3, the caption reads "crates at year 20 · same 2% raise," and the rows have shrunk by different amounts. Frames 4–6 add the totals. Edna still has 10 crates, Ruth has about 9, and Carl has about 4.

3. A fixed 2% raise protects buying power well only if actual inflation stays at or below about 2%. In 1949–1969, Edna's inflation was low, so her income held up. Ruth's 2006–2026 stretch was moderate, so she lost a little. Carl's 1966–1986 stretch included the high inflation of the 1970s, so his purchasing power fell by more than half, even though he got the same raise. The outcome depends on the inflation that happens during retirement, not on the size of the raise.

4. The animation doesn't say what to do, but a viewer could take away a few things. A fixed payment, or one with a small fixed raise, carries inflation risk. It is worth asking whether an income annuity's payments rise with inflation, such as through a cost-of-living adjustment. A viewer might also compare the starting payout of a level option with that of an inflation-adjusted option, which is usually lower. For a 64-year-old who could live 20 or more years, the gap between those two options matters. The animation doesn't show the annuity quote or any numbers for it.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the three cases and the crate counts. It gives no recommendation, and it explicitly says it is not a forecast.
